ny_a_beginning_of_cliff_to_gelsa.blurb: The first stretch of the Near Trapps, the cliff that faces the Trapps across the highway in the Gunks. The rock is the region's hard quartz conglomerate, and the climbing is almost all traditional: horizontal breaks, roofs and steady face moves on cliffs that run from short to a couple hundred feet. The grades are spread wide, from easy fives through the 5.10 to 5.12 range, so both moderate parties and harder leaders find something. The north end of the Nears is the busiest part. Ratings in the Gunks run stiff, and protection is often good but needs hunting for.
ny_a_beginning_of_cliff_to_gelsa.parking_note: Use the West Trapps lot, up the hill from the visitor center past the hairpin and the steel bridge. From the bridge, a trail drops into the woods beneath the Near Trapps.

ny_d_closure_to_harvest_moon.blurb: A section of the Near Trapps, the Gunks cliff across the highway from the main Trapps wall. Climbing here is all traditional, on horizontal-break faces and roofs typical of the ridge, with heights from short up to a couple hundred feet. The grades lean moderate: most routes fall between about 5.7 and 5.9, with a smaller number of easier lines and a few 5.10s and 5.11s, which makes it a fair place for leaders stepping up. Gunks ratings run stiff, and fall weekends are the busiest time.
ny_d_closure_to_harvest_moon.parking_note: Park in the West Trapps lot, reached by climbing the road past the hairpin turn and the steel bridge. Walk back over the bridge toward the Near Trapps trail.

ny_a1_the_uberfall_left.blurb: The first rock you reach walking north from the steel bridge along the Trapps carriage road, and one of the most social spots in the Gunks. Most routes start nearly at road level on the ridge's quartz conglomerate, with roofs, face climbing and horizontal cracks. Nearly everything is traditional, with grades from 5.2 up to 5.12 and a lot of the volume between 5.5 and 5.10. Several routes finish at fixed anchors, but many others need a walk-off, so learn the descent trail before you go. Expect crowds on fall and spring weekends and a full lot early.
ny_a1_the_uberfall_left.parking_note: Leave the car in the West Trapps lot, past the hairpin and the steel bridge. Walk down to the bridge, cross it, and the Uberfall is the first cliff up the carriage road.

_expect.name: The Yellow Wall and The Seasons

ny_j_the_yellow_wall_and_the_seasons.blurb: A steep, orange-tinged section of the Trapps well north of the Uberfall, reached by a side trail through talus off the carriage road. The rock is the Gunks' hard conglomerate, and the climbing is traditional on overhangs, roofs and long face lines. It is a harder-leaning wall: most routes are 5.9 and up, with a good number in the 5.11 and 5.12 range, though a handful of easier climbs exist. Being farther from the Uberfall, it tends to be less crowded. Ratings are stiff and gear can be thin on the steeper pitches.
ny_j_the_yellow_wall_and_the_seasons.parking_note: Use the West Trapps lot, then walk back over the steel bridge and north along the carriage road. It is a longer walk than for the Uberfall, so allow extra time.

ny_h_the_arrow_wall_cck.blurb: A tall stretch of the Trapps best known for multi-pitch trad lines on the Gunks' horizontal-break conglomerate, with roofs and bold face sections. The grades center on 5.8 to 5.10, with fewer easier climbs and a smaller group of 5.11 and harder routes at the top end. Many lines run two or three pitches, so plan on rope management and a walk-off or rappel at the top. Weekends in fall are crowded. Ratings run stiff here, so a route labelled 5.8 can feel solid, and protection often requires careful placements.
ny_h_the_arrow_wall_cck.parking_note: Park in the West Trapps lot and walk the carriage road north from the steel bridge. A climbers' trail climbs through the talus to the base of the wall.

ny_rock_city_state_forest.blurb: A state forest in Cattaraugus County where blocks of conglomerate the size of houses form a maze of alleys, caves and passages. The climbing is almost entirely bouldering, with a few top-rope walls, spread over several pockets: the main city near the loop, a rim trail with harder problems, and a farther Summer Camp zone with longer lines and traverses. Grades run mostly V1 through V4, with a scattering of harder problems, so it suits moderate boulderers well. The forest is wooded and can stay damp, and the access road is a seasonal dirt track, which can lengthen the walk in cold months.
ny_rock_city_state_forest.parking_note: From Route 219 take Hungry Hollow Road, then follow the dirt Little Rock City road to the parking loop near its end. The boulders are a short hike from there.

ny_eagle_falls.blurb: A remote riverside crag in the western Adirondacks, beside the Beaver River below Beaver Lake. Both bolted and traditional lines climb the faces, aretes and big roofs above the rapids. The rock is brittle in places and cracks can be loose, though hidden holds make the faces rewarding. Grades span easy fives to the 5.12 and 5.13 range, with the most weight between 5.9 and 5.12. Most routes face southwest or west and get sun in the afternoon. The river is loud enough to make communication hard, and reaching the crag can involve a river crossing or a longer trail from the north.
ny_eagle_falls.approach: From the grassy pull-off on the north side, follow a red-marked old logging road down for roughly a mile.
ny_eagle_falls.parking_note: The standard approach uses a dirt road signed for the Beaver River canoe route, with parking near a large green pipe. A longer northern approach avoids the river crossing.
